    According to recent reports, the new budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    According to recent reports, that changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Big Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    Industry observers note that RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s significant local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

    In a recent development, there’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    Sources indicate that “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan stated. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    In the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    Industry observers note that but News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    According to recent reports, the Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Debuted in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results indicated the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    It has been revealed that “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    In a recent development, many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

    Sources indicate that some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    It has been revealed that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile people and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).
    • For years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps.
    • Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Nov. 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile people and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).

    For years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps. When a person opened a sitemap URL in a browser, Chrome executed that XSLT file to transform the underlying XML code into a clean, clickable HTML table.

    Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    In a recent development, search engines do not use XSLT. Googlebot, Bingbot, and other web crawlers fetch and parse the raw XML nodes (, ) at the source. Crawlers avoid browser-side stylesheets, meaning indexing, crawl efficiency, and search rankings remain unaffected.

    Industry observers note that because Chrome 158 lands while Google’s November core update, which began on Nov. 10, is still rolling, site owners and clients checking their domains during routine ranking audits may panic when they see raw XML in place of the familiar formatted table.

    Depending on your site configuration, WordPress serves its sitemap index from one of two primary URLs:.

    If you open either URL in Chrome 158 or a newer release, seeing a wall of XML tags confirms the browser skipped the XSLT stylesheet, not that the sitemap file is corrupt or broken.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    To verify, or prove to a nervous client, that Google reads the sitemap without trouble, check Google Search Console:.

    As long as Search Console reports “Success,” Google parses the XML structure without error.

    It has been revealed that XML sitemaps exist for machine consumption, and search engine bots read the underlying and tags. Dropping visual styling changes nothing about URL discovery, crawl budget, or search visibility.

    Because Chrome 158 arrives alongside the November core update, clients or stakeholders who inspect their sitemap URLs will spot unformatted XML code and assume a site outage or plugin failure caused ranking fluctuations.

    Industry observers note that chrome logs a deprecation warning in DevTools whenever a page invokes an .xsl stylesheet. Automated site-health crawlers or QA tools that monitor browser console errors may flag sitemap URLs until plugins or WordPress core drop the stylesheet reference.

    Editors and junior marketers who relied on opening /sitemap_index.xml in Chrome as a quick directory of site URLs lose that visual table unless they switch browsers (such as Firefox or Safari, which retain XSLT for the time being) or use a dedicated HTML sitemap.

    Because search crawlers ignore XSLT, you don’t need to rush to make emergency fixes. Choose from the steps below based on your role and client needs:.

    Sources indicate that note: This is only a visual change. Chrome 158’s removal of XSLT support only affects how sitemaps render in human browsers. Search engine crawlers process raw XML directly and are completely unaffected.

    Industry observers note that organic performance, indexing, and rankings remain safe. WordPress 7.2 will remove the stylesheet reference and, with it, the Chrome warnings, leaving core sitemaps as plain XML. Yoast SEO 28.9 will restore a styled view using CSS, while Rank Math and AIOSEO have not confirmed a change.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Software Engineer, AI Tooling Infrastructure to join our AI Tooling team and help build and run the backend services behind Supabase’s AI products. The Supabase MCP server is one example of what the team runs in production, alongside the services that support agent skills and the dashboard assistant. You’ll work closely with the Platform, SRE, Auth, Billing and Edge Functions teams, and with the engineers on the AI Tooling team who build the product surfaces.

    It has been revealed that the AI Tooling team runs its own services in production and carries its own on-call. Traffic from AI clients and agents behaves differently from traffic from people: hundreds of calls a minute, retry loops, and no reading of deprecation warnings. This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

    Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

    Define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

    According to recent reports, participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

    Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring issues into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

    Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

    Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

    Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

    Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

    Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

    Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

    Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

    Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

    Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

    Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

    Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

    Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

    Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

    Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving swiftly.

    It has been revealed that pick your centre of gravity. We expect you to be deep in at least one of these, and to tell us which:.

    APIs and auth: You have designed permission models, token scopes or OAuth flows for third-party or machine clients, and you have migrated them without breaking users.

    Operations: You have run production services yourself: carried the pager, written alerts and runbooks, used SLOs or similar to decide what to fix, and made shared systems less risky over time.

    Gateways and distributed systems: You have built or run proxies or gateways, or debugged hard failures across services (retries, partial failures, upstream outages, fail-open vs fail-closed decisions), and you can reason about load and degradation.

    Experience with agent tooling (MCP or similar), or serving traffic from AI agents and LLM clients.

    Experience moving a service out of a larger codebase while keeping existing clients working.

    Experience with Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Logflare or a similar observability stack, and real SLO work.

    Open-source contributions, especially to Node.js, Go, TypeScript or API tooling.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire firm gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    In a recent development, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Industry observers note that RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    In a recent development, for a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    It has been revealed that “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    Industry observers note that LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

    OpenNews mentioned in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    According to recent reports, the future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism noted Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he noted. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    • Sources indicate that the post describes a two-phase lifecycle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the viral version of Google’s latest research post states the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their company. On Oct. 27, Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni of Google Research published the sleep framework, a method that gives a language model a scheduled offline phase in which it moves what it picked up during use into its long-term weights, then rehearses on data it generates for itself. The viral framing is wrong in a specific way: the post states that the method operates within a fixed architecture under human-defined training rules, so nothing is modifying itself without supervision. What that framing misses is the part that matters here. If this design ships, the knowledge inside Google’s models stops being frozen at a cutoff and starts updating on a cycle that nobody outside Google will see.

    In March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing notable claims to land before major training runs. That advice assumed the cutoff was a wall with a date on it. This paper describes a wall that moves on its own schedule, without a date, and the right way to read it is as the next form of the Google revision: one that changes what the model believes rather than how the index is ranked, and that arrives with no announcement because there is no event to announce.

    Sources indicate that the post describes a two-phase lifecycle. During a wake phase, the model takes input and holds new information in fast, short-term memory components, which is roughly what context does today. During a sleep phase, it stops taking input and runs two stages. The first is consolidation. The model unlocks new, previously dormant low-rank experts inside a mixture-of-experts layout, assigns them to slower-updating memory blocks, and distills the short-term traces into them through a process the authors call knowledge seeding, which in plain terms means the new facts get their own fresh parameters rather than being written over old ones. Then the temporary parameters are reset so the capacity can be reused. The second stage is what the authors call dreaming. The model generates synthetic samples by randomly routing across its experts so that knowledge from different domains mixes, filters those samples with a gradient-based selection method, and fine-tunes on the ones that survive.

    The reported results come from four settings: sequential translation into languages the model had never seen, where standard fine-tuning and in-context approaches forgot earlier languages, and the sleep model held a near-zero performance drop; recall on a long-context benchmark out to ten million tokens; factual knowledge incorporation from document passages, where the sleep model beat supervised fine-tuning and a prior self-editing method; and math reasoning on an open 8-billion-parameter base model. The underlying paper has been on arXiv since June and on OpenReview since September 2025, so the blog post is Google deciding to say this out loud, not Google discovering it.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not a one-off. The same authors published Nested Learning in November 2025 with the Hope architecture and the idea of a continuum memory system, a chain of memory blocks that update at different frequencies, with the fast blocks holding short-term information and the slow blocks holding durable knowledge. The sleep framework is what you build once you have blocks that update at different rates: a schedule for moving information from the fast ones to the slow ones. Titans came before Hope, Hope came before sleep, and the arc now runs about two years. The autoregressive ranking paper I covered in September closed a five-year arc on how results get ordered. This one is younger and just as deliberate.

    It is research, not a product. The post makes no statement about deployment, timelines, or which Google models might use it. The experiments run on open Qwen models at 1.7 and 8 billion parameters, not on Gemini. No compute cost is reported for a sleep cycle, and no one outside the team has replicated the results. In the experiments, the new facts arrive as documents, not as user conversations or crawled web pages, so anyone claiming the model learns from your chats is extrapolating past the paper.

    Those caveats are real and they do not change things. Google publishes research arcs and then ships pieces of them, and that pattern has held often enough that the practitioner question is not whether this exact method lands but what the design tells you about the direction. The direction is a model whose long-term memory is rewritten on a cycle.

    Anyone who has done this work for more than a few years lived through the first version of this shift. Google says it updates Search thousands of times a year and shares only the ones it considers notable, and in a 2022 interview Danny Sullivan put the previous year’s experiments and quality tests above 800,000. The named core updates are the handful that get a dashboard entry. Everything else lands continuously and silently, and the industry adapted by building a diagnostic ritual around the named few: traffic moves, you check the date against the revision trackers, and attribution follows.

    Retrieval already took the same path for freshness. AI Overviews and grounded answers pull new pages daily with nothing unveiled, so a claim that silence is new would be wrong. What the sleep framework changes is which layer goes silent. Retrieval changes what the model can look up. Consolidation changes what the model believes without looking anything up. Those are different things for a brand. A retrieved fact is cited, hedged, and replaceable the next time the page is fetched. A consolidated fact is spoken with the confidence of something the model knows, and the March piece covered why that confidence difference shapes how a brand appears in an answer.

    Industry observers note that so the shape practitioners already know, declared core updates on the outside and unannounced tweaks between them, gets a second copy one layer down: announced model versions on the outside, unannounced consolidation accumulating between them. The ranking stack does not go away and this does not replace it. It sits on top of it, in the model that writes the answer.

    The detail in the post I keep returning to is that consolidation is selective. The authors say the model is not asked to copy every detail from its short-term traces into its parameters, and the dreaming stage scores its own samples with a gradient-based filter before anything is trained on. That is a ranking function. It decides which facts the model will carry forward as durable knowledge and which it will let expire with the temporary parameters. Being seen during wake is not being learned. Being learned is what being indexed used to mean, and the thing deciding it is a loss calculation nobody outside Google can inspect.

    Three consequences follow, and the first two are my inference from the design rather than claims the paper makes.

    First, the filter will favor facts that are consistent across sources. A gradient-based selection method keeps samples that reduce error broadly, and a fact that agrees with everything else the model has seen reduces error more reliably than one that contradicts a competitor’s page, a stale directory listing, or your own older content. Conflicting versions of your company are no longer only a conflation risk at retrieval time, which I covered when German courts started holding the platform responsible for false answers, but a consolidation risk, because the version that gets learned is the one that fits best, not the one you prefer.

    Second, dreaming means the model rehearses on data you never published. The synthetic samples are generated by mixing experts across domains, so the model’s representation of a company can shift through rehearsal with no upcoming input from anyone. No competitor moved, no page changed, no upgrade ran, and the answer about you is different anyway. This is a candidate mechanism for a question I have been asked repeatedly this year, which is why an answer changed when nothing observable changed.

    Recent findings suggest that third, and this one sits in the paper’s design directly, there is a window. Between a fact entering the fast memory and the next consolidation, a correction is cheap because nothing durable has been written yet. After consolidation, fixing a false fact is no longer a matter of updating a page and waiting for a recrawl. It is unlearning, and removing one specific fact from a model’s weights without damaging the rest remains an open research problem. The term I would use is the consolidation window, the period in which a wrong fact can still be caught before the model commits it, and the uncomfortable property of the window is that its length and timing are unknown to you.

    If no Google model announcement within roughly 18 months references periodic updates between releases, continual learning in production, or anything resembling a consolidation cycle, this stays a research direction, and the cutoff stays a wall. If the compute cost of a sleep cycle turns out to be comparable to a training run, the economics kill the cadence idea even if the method works. And if Google chooses to publish consolidation events the way it publishes core updates, the silence argument fails and the diagnostic ritual survives with a new row on the dashboard. I think the third is the least likely of the three, because Google has never published its unnamed changes and has said plainly that it does not intend to.

    The useful response is to stop building process around an event that may stop existing.

    The cutoff-aware calendaring I suggested in March still holds for the next major training run, because those will keep happening. What changes is the half-life of the word parametric. The safest assumption is that what the model knows about you is being revised on a schedule you cannot see, by a filter you cannot inspect, and that the only observable is the answer itself.

    This post was originally published on Duane Forrester Decodes.

    21 Alternative Search Engines You Can Use Instead of Google via @sejournal, @lorenbaker

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that for many people, searching the web means opening Google.
    • Industry observers note that but the search engine you use out of habit is not always the best tool for the job.
    • It has been revealed that that is where alternatives earn their place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that for many people, searching the web means opening Google. It’s a familiar place to research a purchase, check a fact, or catch up on the news and that reach demonstrates in the numbers with Google accounting for 91.04% of worldwide search engine referrals according to Statcounter in October 2026.

    Industry observers note that but the search engine you use out of habit is not always the best tool for the job. Think about the last time you needed an image you could reuse, a webpage that had disappeared, or a more private way to search. Those are different problems, and a single search box is not always the easiest way to solve them.

    It has been revealed that that is where alternatives earn their place. Some give you more control over privacy and rankings, whilst others bring together sources in a conversation, search a specialist collection, or help you explore the content people use in another country. For marketers, those differences also explain why visibility beyond Google involves more than submitting a website to another engine.

    You don’t have to give up Google to find out what you might be missing. We collated 21 alternative search engines and tools worth trying, whether you’re looking for a better answer or a new way for customers to find your business.

    About the Usage Figures: Entries are ordered within each section by estimated monthly visits to the named website or subdomain. The October 2026 figures are not unique users, search queries, or app activity. Statcounter percentages shown separately measure search referral share, not visits.

    Industry observers note that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 6 billion to chatgpt.com, October 2026. This covers the ChatGPT website, not Search alone.

    ChatGPT is useful when your question needs a conversation rather than a fresh set of keywords each time. You can ask it to compare two approaches, explain an unfamiliar term, and then look for recent evidence without starting over. Its advantage is keeping the context of that investigation together.

    Industry observers note that openAI’s search documentation says it can retrieve current web information and link to sources. Search is available on free and paid plans, including for people who are not signed in, although usage limits apply. ChatGPT may search automatically, or you can select Search from its tools.

    Use it to work through a question, then open the citations to check the answer. It can misread a source or miss a qualification, and its use of other search providers means it is not simply a separate, independent web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 88.3 million to perplexity.ai, October 2026.

    Perplexity puts source-backed answers at the center of the search experience. Its research-oriented approach is useful when you want an overview of a subject and a trail of sources to investigate, rather than opening a long list of results before finding the main points.

    Its Pro Search process can conduct multiple searches and bring findings together, with follow-up questions keeping the research in context. Depending on your blueprint, you can narrow the work to areas such as academic or financial sources. Access and limits vary by tier.

    The benefit is a faster route into a topic, not a substitute for reading the evidence. Check that each citation supports the statement beside it because AI answers can still contain hallucinations even when links are present.

    Why SEO Experts Should Care: Perplexity can be useful even if it sends less traffic than Google. In his post on why marketers should care about Perplexity, Dennis Goedegebuure argues that it is a low-cost test bench for AI search. Try the research questions your customers ask, inspect which pages get cited, and check how your brand and recently updated facts appear. For B2B marketers, that means testing visibility during product research, rather than judging the opportunity solely by overall visit totals.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.7 billion to bing.com, October 2026.

    According to recent reports, bing is a full-service alternative for everyday web, image, video, and news searches. One concrete reason to try it is Visual Search: when you have a picture of a product, plant, or object but do not know its name, you can start with the image instead of guessing keywords.

    According to recent reports, microsoft’s visual search tools can find related images and shopping options, identify objects, and extract or translate text from a picture. Conventional results remain available alongside AI-assisted tools, so an answer does not have to be the end of your search.

    Search Engine Journal covered Bing’s search updates in December 2024, including work on faster, more precise results. Try the same image or video query on Bing and Google to see which makes the next step easier for you; that is more useful than assuming one wins every search.

    Where available, Bing’s Copilot Search adds AI-generated summaries with source citations and suggested follow-up topics, so you can explore a question without starting from scratch.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 751 million to search.yahoo.com, October 2026.

    It has been revealed that search Engine Referral Share: 2.54% in the U.S., October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Yahoo Search makes the most sense if you already use Yahoo for news, finance, or other daily information. Its value is the connection between search and that wider content ecosystem, rather than a completely different index of the web.

    Yahoo introduced Scout in January 2026 as an AI answer engine combining open-web information with Yahoo content and data. The U.S. beta launch named Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft’s Bing grounding API as parts of the system.

    That gives Yahoo owners a way to move from a headline or financial topic into a sourced explanation. You can still browse traditional search results, and you should follow Scout’s source links when an answer matters. The launch’s audience figures cover Yahoo’s broader services, not people using Scout alone.

    Recent findings suggest that at Search Engine Journal, Yahoo accounts for about 0.2% of our traffic. It’s a small share, but it still brings a few thousand visits in a month and for a different business, even that smaller stream of visitors could include a potential customer or lead to a sale.

    Industry observers note that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.7 billion to baidu.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    Industry observers note that search Engine Referral Share: 49% in China, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Baidu matters when your research or marketing is aimed at Chinese-language audiences. Its value is not simply in translating an English query, but it offers a view of Chinese-language search and a connected set of local content services.

    Alongside web results, its homepage links to maps, images, video, the Baike encyclopedia, Zhidao questions and answers, and Wenku documents. Those services give you distinct places to investigate how a topic, product, or brand is described. Use the terminology that local sources use rather than assuming an English search will surface the same material.

    Industry observers note that for marketers, the search referral share is a reason to investigate Baidu separately, not proof that it will send a particular site traffic. Distinguish content hosted inside Baidu’s services from results linking to external publishers, and assess the original source.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.5 billion to naver.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 42.25% in South Korea, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Sources indicate that naver is useful for Korean-language research because its search experience brings together more than external webpages. Naver’s search overview describes results across news, maps, cafés, blogs, images, video, and other categories.

    Sources indicate that that mix gives you a route into local experiences and community content as well as conventional reporting. Its community services include Naver Blog, interest-based Café communities, and Knowledge iN questions and answers. If you are researching a Korean product or audience, those are different sources to explore from an English-language web-results page.

    For website owners, Naver Search Advisor is the official starting point for webmaster tools. Keep visits to an external website separate from engagement with a blog or other content hosted inside Naver.

    In a recent development, estimated Monthly Web Visits: 162.2 million to yandex.com, October 2026. This covers the international website, not total use across all Yandex domains.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 70.22% in Russia, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Yandex is worth checking when you need Russian-language sources or are researching visibility in Russia. Its large share of measured referrals there gives it a different role from a small global alternative – it is an notable regional search environment in its own right.

    Industry observers note that use it to compare which local publishers and pages appear for the terminology your audience actually uses. Its international homepage also presents an AI search option, but the practical reason to investigate it is the regional results and audience context, not simply another chatbot interface.

    Industry observers note that SEJ’s Yandex guide provides background for marketers. The 2023 data leak is a separate historical event, not a verified description of today’s ranking system. The search referral share above describes referrals, not the percentage of Russian people using Yandex.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 16.5 million to sogou.com, October 2026.

    Sogou offers another route into Chinese-language information, with a more specific reason to try it rather than simply comparing general web results – its WeChat search is a destination for discovering public accounts and articles from that ecosystem.

    Sources indicate that that is useful when the material you need was published as a WeChat article rather than an ordinary standalone webpage. Search in the relevant Chinese terminology and distinguish those public articles from results in Sogou’s general web search.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not access to private messages or every piece of content in WeChat. As with other platform-specific searches, check the account, publication date, and original article before using a result as evidence.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 698.8 million to search.brave.com, October 2026.

    In a recent development, brave Search combines an independent web index with tools for changing how results are ranked. It is worth trying if you want both an alternative to Google or Bing’s underlying results and more say over which sources rise to the top.

    According to recent reports, its search help describes Goggles, which apply alternative ranking or filtering rules. Brave also describes domain-level ranking controls and an AI answer experience on its about page. Those controls give you something more specific to experiment with than a different-looking results page.

    SEJ reported Brave’s Bing separation in 2023. You can use Brave Search in another browser, so testing its index does not require adopting Brave’s browser, wallet, VPN, or other products.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 681.9 million to duckduckgo.com, October 2026.

    DuckDuckGo is a straightforward choice if you want everyday search without a personal search-history profile. You can use its search website in your existing browser, so the switch does not require changing your whole browsing setup.

    Privacy and index independence are different benefits, however. DuckDuckGo’s source documentation states traditional links and images largely come from Bing, supplemented by specialist sources, its own crawler, and its own indexes. Choose it for that privacy model, not on the assumption that every result comes from a separate web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 57.6 million to startpage.com, October 2026.

    Industry observers note that startpage is for people who want results from major search providers without dealing with those providers directly. It acts as a privacy intermediary, submitting your query on your behalf and returning the results to you.

    In a recent development, its partner explanation identifies both Google and Microsoft Bing. Startpage notes it does not share personal information with them, and that those providers see Startpage rather than the person making the request.

    That is the distinction from an independent-index engine: Startpage changes the relationship between you and the search provider, not necessarily the underlying collection of pages. It is worth trying if you like familiar results but want a different privacy arrangement; it is not a way to avoid Google’s infrastructure altogether.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.6 million to kagi.com, October 2026.

    Its Lenses let you narrow searches to selected websites or categories such as forums, academic sources, or PDFs. Kagi’s source documentation describes its own indexes alongside major and specialist providers, with an emphasis on surfacing independent and noncommercial content. It is not powered solely by its Teclis index.

    As of November 2026, its monthly individual looks include Starter at $5 plus tax for 300 searches and Professional at $10 plus tax for unlimited searches. Annual billing has different terms. If you search heavily and want persistent control over sources, those features are the reason to consider paying.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 219 million to ecosia.org, October 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that ecosia lets you put the revenue from an everyday habit toward climate work. It notes all of its profits go to climate action, with the majority funding tree-planting projects. That is its central reason to exist: changing who benefits financially from search.

    The company publishes monthly financial reports, so you can look beyond the tree counter to see how money is spent. Its provider documentation lists Bing, Google, and European Search Perspective, or EUSP; the mix depends on factors including region, device, and permissions.

    This makes Ecosia a funding-model choice, not a promise that every query uses a wholly separate index. If you want to support its mission while keeping familiar web search, it is a low-friction option to try. You can check the provider through the information control beside a result.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 451,800 to karmasearch.org, October 2026.

    Sources indicate that KARMA applies the search-funded nonprofit model to animal welfare and biodiversity. Its distinction from a broader climate-focused service is the cause: helping fund organizations working on wildlife, habitats, and animal protection.

    Recent findings suggest that the firm’s explanation notes sponsored search links generate revenue for its nonprofit partners. Its site lists partners including Re:wild, Humane World for Animals, and iNaturalist. You can inspect those partnerships to decide whether they match the work you want to support.

    It has been revealed that availability varies by country. During this review, a U.S. capture showed the search homepage, while a visit from another region displayed a notice that KARMA was unavailable there and would redirect searches to Bing. Check local availability before making it your default; a regional restriction does not mean the service has closed.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 155,800 to yep.com, October 2026.

    According to recent reports, yep is an Ahrefs-built alternative with a distinctive audience beyond people typing into a search box: developers who want web results for an AI agent or research application. Ahrefs’ current Yep product page describes a first-party crawler, index, and ranking system, with result excerpts and filters for the information an application retrieves.

    Recent findings suggest that the public search interface captured for this review also returned conventional web results. For an everyday user, that makes it another index to compare; for a developer, the API is the clearer reason to investigate it. The current homepage emphasizes that developer-facing use rather than presenting a Google-like consumer pitch.

    SEJ’s 2022 Yep interview explains the original proposal to share advertising revenue with creators. Although, the current homepage does not establish that those proposed payouts are operating, so they should not be the reason you choose it today.

    Industry observers note that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.4 billion to x.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    x.com is useful when the thing you need is a public statement or conversation: what an organization announced, what a named person said, or how a developing event is being discussed. You are searching posts on the platform, not a general index of webpages.

    Industry observers note that that direct access to posted statements is its advantage for news monitoring and research. Its advanced search is a further option for signed-in users; the public Explore route redirected to a sign-in screen during this review.

    Recent findings suggest that use posts to locate leads and original statements, not as automatic confirmation of a claim. Check the account, timestamp, and supporting evidence, especially when an old post is circulating as if it describes a fresh event.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 2.1 billion to linkedin.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    Industry observers note that linkedIn is useful when your search starts with a professional identity, such as a person, employer, role, or job. It can also help you find practitioners discussing a work-related subject, rather than only the publishers ranking for that subject on the open web.

    The advantage is the professional context. A name alongside an employer and career history gives you a way to distinguish people who share a name and identify a relevant source. Its public people search is one starting point, although fuller profiles and other features can require signing in.

    Recent findings suggest that treat profiles as self-reported information, not a verified tech giant directory. Check current roles and dates against the person’s or organization’s own website when those details matter to your research.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 46.4 million to web.archive.org, October 2026.

    The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine answers a question a current search result often cannot: What did this webpage say before it changed or disappeared? It is useful for checking an old product claim, recovering a removed reference, or following the history of a website.

    According to recent reports, enter the URL and inspect the available captures. The advantage is the dated record where you can compare versions rather than relying on a current page to explain its own past. Check the capture date and whether images and other resources were preserved.

    Sources indicate that the Wayback Machine is part of the wider Internet Archive, whose books, recordings, software, and other collections are separate resources. It is not a complete archive of every page, and a captured claim is evidence of what a page said then, not proof that the claim was true.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 39.3 million to slideshare.net, October 2026.

    SlideShare is worth trying when you want the presentation itself, not another article summarizing the subject. A conference talk, research deck, or business pitch can reveal how someone structures an argument and illustrates the details.

    The current homepage describes a collection of more than 25 million presentations. Browsing, reading, and uploading do not require a subscription, while features such as downloading presentations are paid benefits. The value is a format-specific collection you can explore for research or presentation inspiration.

    Check the uploader and publication date before relying on a deck’s statistics or recommendations. Being able to view a presentation also does not automatically give you permission to reuse its artwork.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.1 million to wolframalpha.com, October 2026.

    Sources indicate that wolframAlpha is for questions that need computation rather than a list of pages. If you want to solve an equation, convert units, or work with structured facts, it can calculate an answer from its data and algorithms instead of leaving you to find a suitable calculator elsewhere.

    It has been revealed that its explanation of the service describes dynamic computation over curated knowledge. The mathematics examples show the inputs it understands; other areas include science, dates, and measures.

    That is a different job from comparing recent reporting or finding an opinion. Use it when the result should be computed, and check how it interpreted your units, assumptions, and wording before relying on the output.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 296,200 to openverse.org, October 2026.

    Openverse is the tool to try when finding a usable image or audio track matters more than finding a webpage about one. It focuses on openly licensed and public-domain media, making it useful for an article, presentation, or other creative project.

    Recent findings suggest that its About page describes a collection of more than 800 million images and audio tracks gathered from multiple repositories, with features such as one-click attribution. That collection size is separate from its website traffic. Its advantage is bringing reuse-oriented discovery into one place, rather than treating every image on the web as equally available to use.

    Recent findings suggest that openly licensed does not mean free of conditions. Licenses can require attribution or restrict commercial use, and Openverse does not verify every work’s licensing information. Follow through to the original source and confirm the license before using a file.

    Sources indicate that the introduction of ChatGPT helped bring conversational interfaces into everyday use. In January 2023, SEJ reported that Google’s founders had responded by returning to discussions about its AI response and then opened access to Bard in March 2023.

    Google rolled out AI Overviews to U.S. users in May 2024 and revealed AI Mode in 2025. Those developments explain why many services in this list now combine web results with AI generated answers. The two formats can help with different parts of the same research task.

    Google may be the most familiar option, but the best choice for a particular task can be different. Try a few real queries on two or three services, compare the sources, the ease of finding the original information, and the controls you will actually use.

    Industry observers note that you can keep one engine for everyday searches and use another for a specific job. A calculation, an archived webpage, and a professional profile do not need to start in the same search box.

    Featured Image: Igor Link/Shutterstock.

    Industry observers note that open your browser’s search settings and choose a supported default engine. If the service is not listed, use its official browser setup instructions. You can also visit its website directly without changing your default.

    Start with the task you want to improve. Try Bing for general web search, DuckDuckGo for a search service centered on privacy, Brave Search for another independent index, and ChatGPT or Perplexity for conversational answers. Compare their results on queries you already know well.

    Some do. Startpage identifies Google and Bing as partners. DuckDuckGo largely sources traditional links and images from Bing. Kagi combines its own indexes with several providers. Brave Search builds an independent web index.

    No. DuckDuckGo claims it is an independent manufacturer. A search provider relationship is different from ownership, and its traditional links and images largely come from Bing.

    No search tool can guarantee a neutral view of everything online. Index coverage, ranking rules, filters, location, and the query itself affect what appears. Compare independent sources and more than one search engine when the differences matter.

    Business models vary. Some display search advertising, some charge subscriptions, and some combine free and paid services. Read the specific service’s policy because a privacy claim does not mean every product, advertisement, and linked website handles data in the same way.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Supabase already spreads from the bottom up: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.About the Role.

    We’re looking for a Product Manager, Administration & Governance to join our Product Team and make Supabase the default starting point for software built inside a company.

    Supabase already spreads from the bottom up: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. Inside most companies, Supabase starts the same way: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. The next step is making that momentum firm-wide: one platform where anyone can start building, and where IT can see what’s running, who owns it, and what it costs.

    You’ll own how companies run Supabase as their internal development platform: approved by IT and easy for anyone in the manufacturer to use. You’ll make it possible for people and the agents they work with to start building without waiting on infrastructure, while giving platform, IT, and security teams the controls they need to say yes. The goal is to make the approved path the easiest path, from an early experiment to a production application, with the controls companies need built in.

    Own the product strategy and roadmap for internal innovation, from a manufacturer’s first IT-approved rollout to adoption across teams and business units.

    It has been revealed that make getting started self-service, whether someone creates a project in Supabase, through an internal developer portal, or with an agent. Give builders the access and infrastructure they need without a ticket for every project.

    Steer scattered usage into a manageable company-wide platform. Give companies one view of everything they run on Supabase. Shape how ownership, delegated access, and boundaries work so teams can move independently as usage grows.

    Industry observers note that partner closely with platform, IT, security, and finance teams to understand what it takes to approve Supabase and keep it approved. Translate their needs into practical identity, policy, audit, and spend controls that don’t slow builders down.

    Define the path from experiment to production, including project ownership, access, and the guardrails that change as an application becomes notable to the business.

    Work with Engineering, Design, Sales, and Customer Success to turn early customer rollouts into a repeatable experience, rather than a upcoming custom integration for every manufacturer.

    Define what success looks like, instrument it end to end, and let the data guide what gets built next—from time to first project and self-service adoption to production usage and expansion across the tech giant.

    Have 7+ years of product management on developer tools, infrastructure, or internal developer platforms.

    Have built self-service products that developers love and platform or IT teams trust. You understand both the person trying to ship an app and the team responsible for how it runs.

    Can reason about identity, permissions, organization boundaries, and usage attribution, and turn those systems into workflows people can actually understand.

    Have a strong point of view on how agents change who can build software inside a firm and what an internal development platform needs to make that possible.

    Know your way around controlled experimentation and data analysis, and can connect easier adoption to sustained product use.

    Are biased toward speed and would rather ship, learn, and iterate than perfect a spec.

    Build with what you own and form opinions through first-hand use, from creating a project to configuring the policies around it.

    Use AI tools to compress research, drafting, and feedback synthesis so you can focus on judgment calls.

    Work async by default, making decisions in writing in a fully remote team.

    It has been revealed that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    According to recent reports, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    According to recent reports, once a year, the entire company gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

    RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

    Recent findings suggest that still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a upcoming website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent company is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney said.

    In Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website people to our news coverage,” Eckenrode stated, and had some success with that strategy.

    Industry observers note that in September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in Latest York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

    On the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” stated Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a new California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a fresh book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist said; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.).
