    #101123. Industry News: Why Building Trust Through Real People Stands The Test Of Time In SEO & AI Search via @sejournal, @lilyraynyc

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4176 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why Building Trust Through Real People Stands The Test Of Time In SEO & AI Search via @sejournal, @lilyraynyc

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that when it comes to organic search marketing, a loophole is not a strategy.
    • Any SEO who has worked in the field for a while has inevitably lived through a seemingly endless loop of fads, hype cycles, and shortcuts aimed at tricking search engines (and now, AI systems).
    • According to recent reports, plenty of people in this industry have battle scars from these experiences, myself included.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that when it comes to organic search marketing, a loophole is not a strategy. Loopholes have expiration dates, and in many cases, the time spent chasing them would have been better spent on work that doesn’t backfire later on.

    Any SEO who has worked in the field for a while has inevitably lived through a seemingly endless loop of fads, hype cycles, and shortcuts aimed at tricking search engines (and now, AI systems). Exact-match domains, article directories, parasite SEO, guest posting at scale, PBNs, programmatic pages, and now the AI-generated listicles, scaled AI content, and “inauthentic mentions” of the GEO era. Most of these things work for a while… until they don’t. And once Google, Bing, and more recently the AI companies themselves crack down, the sites that leaned on these approaches often end up worse off than if they’d never tried them at all, sometimes spending years cleaning up while traffic, visibility, and leads stay suppressed.

    According to recent reports, plenty of people in this industry have battle scars from these experiences, myself included. My first real SEO wins came from buying links in 2010-2011, and Penguin erased them in a single morning in 2012. Six years later, the 2018 “Medic” update hit a client of ours that had been using AI and automation to scale medical content (long before this was popular), and it was the hardest hit from an algorithm update that I had experienced firsthand since the Penguin update. I think these scars are the badge of honor that inevitably comes with experience in SEO: thinking you know better than Google, and learning the hard way that you almost always don’t.

    All of that noted, there is one investment that has held up through every one of those cycles, and it’s the same approach I’ve recommended for many years: investing in real humans and placing them at the center of your marketing strategy. As AI makes generic content nearly free to produce, I believe that real, identifiable experts are becoming the clearest antidote to scaled, machine-generated slop. This article covers why, what the evidence shows so far, and how brands can consider “human-centric marketing” as a bigger part of their strategies.

    The list of spam violations Google laid out back then has carried on, in some form, for more than 20 years, right into the AI search era. I put together this infographic showing how Google’s original spam policies map to popular GEO tactics we see today with AI search:.

    Automation in particular has been in the crosshairs for well over a decade. In August 2010, Google’s John Mueller told a site owner that publishing Google Translate output directly “could be seen as creating auto-generated content, which would be against our Webmaster Guidelines,” and recommended having a human correct it first. By 2012, Google had published a dedicated help page on automatically generated content. Its examples included text “translated by an automated tool without human review or curation,” Markov chains, automated synonymizing, scraped feeds, and “stitching or combining content from different web pages without adding sufficient value.”.

    For what it’s worth, I still see this exact glitch affecting sites today – perhaps more than ever – including companies who come to me after experimenting with scaled AI translations that get little human review. It’s interesting that John’s 15+ year old answer still holds up, although to be fair, most site owners have never read Google’s guidelines (and nobody can be expected to know about a forum reply from 2010). That’s what their SEO experts are (supposedly) there to help them with.

    Funny enough, that 2012 list reads a lot like the sales pitch for the same AI content tools that have recently captured the attention of C-level marketers everywhere, many of which work in ways that come very close to (if not directly violate) Google’s long-standing anti-spam policies. It’s not a huge surprise that so many of the sites featured in their case studies have since rapidly lost organic traffic.

    Google’s wording has evolved since then, but the thread running through it has stayed remarkably consistent. In February 2023, a few months after ChatGPT rolled out, Google remarked it has “many years of experience dealing with automation being used in an attempt to game search results.” Then in March 2024, Google launched the scaled content abuse spam policy, which applies whether content is made “through automation, human efforts, or some combination of human and automated processes.” Automated translation, synonymizing, and stitching are still on the list, 14 years later. Marketers are now using LLMs to experiment heavily with all three. The main difference now is that generative AI sits at the top of the list of examples.

    Across more than 20 years of guidelines, the common thread is fairly simple: content made for search engines at scale, with no human reviewing it, adding to it, or standing behind it, eventually becomes a liability.

    Industry observers note that when Google started using the acronym “E-A-T” in 2014 (now called “E-E-A-T”), it finally gave us a framework that shows how to even do SEO work without getting caught up in the loopholes. Since then, E-E-A-T has been misunderstood, misused, and treated as a checklist or a single ranking factor that works the same way for every site (it doesn’t). In 2021, I even wrote an article aimed specifically at debunking many of these misconceptions.

    According to recent reports, all of that being said, I still to this day believe E-E-A-T is the best framework we have for approaching our SEO/GEO strategies in ways that won’t be penalized or devalued later, and it gives us plenty of meaningful work to do once we focus on the right things. There’s a reason E-E-A-T is mentioned 120 times in the current version of Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines, and why Bing uses similar language, focusing on “quality and credibility,” in its own guidelines.

    Recent findings suggest that this type of work is people-first, meaning actual humans with lived knowledge sit at the center of the approach. It’s much harder than loophole-focused SEO, because it needs buy-in, time, and resources from the experts at the company, not just the SEO team operating behind the scenes. But the return is high, and it affects more channels than just organic. It tends to stand the test of time; it’s good for your users and your conversions; it appears to help with AI systems; and it’s unlikely to get you penalized (unless you apply a shortcut mindset to it, which isn’t really an E-E-A-T strategy at all). It’s also the opposite of what folks publicly say they hate about the impact SEO has had on Google’s results, from The Verge asking whether SEO experts ruined the internet to a 2024 study finding product review results increasingly full of SEO spam.

    I’ve been preaching these same ideas for years, and I probably sound like a broken record to anyone who has followed me for a while (my MozCon 2022 talk was all about how to focus on real expertise, with numerous examples of real experts representing the brands they worked for). I even named my holistic approach to SEO/GEO the E-E-A-T Method and made it the core philosophy of my upcoming consultancy, Algorythmic, because that’s how deeply I believe in the efficacy of this approach.

    But this wasn’t always a massive focus in how I approached SEO; it’s something I learned the hard way.

    That 2018 Medic client I referred to before had been scaling a fast-growing library of health articles with no visible credentials from experts, and no sign of a real human behind any of it. When the upgrade hit, Google’s Danny Sullivan pointed site owners back to the Search Quality Rater Guidelines (his tweet has since been deleted, but Marie Haynes wrote about his guidance at the time). So I spent months reading and re-reading Google’s guidelines. Being the nerd that I am, I even printed and laminated a copy and kept it on my desk (which I admitted on stage in 2019 at BrightonSEO). When I read it, the answer to our client’s challenge became obvious, and it was repeated throughout the guidelines: the site was heavily YMYL (Your Money or Your Life) and showed nowhere near enough E-A-T for the health topics it covered and the medical advice it provided.

    Recent findings suggest that the client wasn’t convinced at first, as this required a dramatic overhaul of their approach – so much so that we decided to part ways while they tried to bring back the site’s performance using their own methods. But after almost two years without recovering, the client came back to work with our team again. We worked together on a renewed SEO strategy, and about six months later, we relaunched the entire site, rebuilt from top to bottom around E-A-T, with human experts at the center: real doctors, real medical reviewers, and their original insights. The site climbed back to its previous levels after the re-platforming was complete. From the day the patch hit, the full recovery process took more than three years. (This long recovery timeline is why I always warn sites to avoid getting hit in the first place!).

    It has been revealed that back in January 2019, the night before my first-ever conference talk at SMX West (which was – surprise! – focused on E-A-T), I sat at the hotel bar studying Mark Traphagen’s work on author authority. He, along with Jennifer Slegg, had been documenting the history of “authorship” and “author authority” on Google over time. (Funny side note: I ended up meeting Mark in person for the first time at the conference breakfast the next morning, a few hours before I went on stage, which felt auspicious.) After my presentation, when an attendee asked what a small site should do if its writers aren’t well known, my answer was to “cultivate your authors’ profiles, even if it means starting from scratch,” which ruffled some feathers in a room filled with technical SEOs who didn’t all buy into the idea that Google could figure these things out. Yet nearly eight years of research and client results later, I’m even more convinced that it can.

    Industry observers note that A few months later, Google’s official guidance on core updates linked to my BrightonSEO deck on E-A-T as a recommended resource, along with work from a few other SEOs. This solidified for me that E-A-T was becoming a big priority for them. In 2020, I had the great privilege of digging into the patents that might explain how E-A-T works with the late, great Bill Slawski, whose knowledge of Google’s patents was unmatched. This exercise helped me understand a more technical explanation for how Google’s systems might recognize individual experts. The following year, I took the topic to the MozCon stage with a talk on how the E-A-T ecosystem has transformed organic search.

    “Humanize your brand” and “keep a human in the loop” have become marketing clichés of their own, so I want to be specific. By “real humans,” I mean practitioners with genuine expertise or experience: the doctor who has treated the condition, the engineer who built the system, the plumber who owns a local plumbing business, or the patient who lived through the illness. They earn their audience naturally, and across platforms, by sharing insights that are honest, original, often opinionated, and based on real experience. You can usually tell them apart from someone who indicated up to sell you something, and if a sale happens at all, it tends to follow from the trust they’ve built.

    Recent findings suggest that my approach, for SEO, AI search, and broader marketing, is to put these real people at the center of the strategy whenever possible. It’s also what I’ve employed with my own personal brand (more on that later).

    Industry observers note that I think this is the strategy most likely to survive whatever comes next, for a simple reason. Nearly every popular shortcut in the vicious cycle of SEO could be scaled. A real expert’s reputation can’t. It takes years of showing up, being right (and sometimes wrong, and open to admitting that) in public, and having other people vouch for you without needing to rely on inauthentic mentions or listicles calling yourself the best expert. As AI makes everything else cheaper to produce, I’d expect the value of that kind of earned reputation to keep climbing.

    In April 2024, on the Authority Hacker podcast, I summed it up with one of the sentences I’ve mentioned most often in my career:.

    “I’ve been talking about this for years: People like following people.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sidenote: Don’t mind the ghost opening the door behind me. That was my dog Marcy, who can never decide where she wants to lie down when I’m doing podcasts.

    Sources indicate that it’s no secret that folks on social platforms engage with other people far more than with brands. On LinkedIn, personal profiles outperform company pages by roughly 2x to 8x on impressions, depending on whose data you believe.

    Here’s what real people bring to the table that AI can’t:.

    Across platforms, signs of a real human may be the clearest way to separate spam and automated content from the content that provides the most value.

    Industry observers note that A real human expert leaves evidence everywhere, and that footprint is easily detectable: photos from the conference they spoke at, video of the talk, a personal website (even a slightly neglected one), podcast interviews, years of social posts and replies, or journalists quoting them by name. I believe Google has systems in place to at least identify these signals, and likely reward them, from Knowledge Panels to the new Search profiles. The leaked Google documentation from May 2024 points in the same direction: it showed that Google stores the author of a document, and has an attribute called isAuthor that marks whether an entity mentioned on a page is also the author of that page.

    The typical fake author, on the other hand, has a stock-looking AI-generated headshot, a two-sentence bio (if any), and no other evidence of their real existence anywhere on the web. This approach isn’t limited to small sites, either: in 2023, Sports Illustrated was found publishing product reviews under authors who didn’t appear to exist, including one whose headshot was for sale on a site that sells AI-generated portraits. In that same year, fake authors were one of the most common patterns I found among sites hit by the Helpful Content Revision, and in October 2026, Google added this exact tactic to its helpful content documentation: “Fabricating creator profiles (such as by using AI-generated headshots, made-up names, or false credentials to make content appear as if it was written by human experts) is a form of deception.”.

    I predict that this trail of being a “real human” will matter even more as the web fills up with homogeneous vibe-coded sites. Anyone can now spin up a polished website in an afternoon, complete with a logo, a hundred blog posts, and a team page full of friendly AI-generated headshots. If you’ve looked at many of these sites, you’ve probably noticed they all start to look the same: the same purple gradient, the same three feature cards with emoji icons, the same “Trusted by” logo strip.

    It has been revealed that when a convincing-looking brand costs next to nothing and takes little time to build, polish alone doesn’t tell anyone very much anymore. What’s left are the signals that still take years to build: a real person or real people with real histories, who other real people have chosen to follow, quote, and recommend.

    It has been revealed that since the 2018 Medic enhancement, Google appears to have spent the past 8 years building systems that reward exactly that kind of trail. In 2019, I analyzed 64 sites that had clearly won or lost across the 2018 and 2019 core updates, checking each one for 30 on-page E-A-T signals and researching the credentials of the people writing their content. The winning sites were 258% more likely than the losing sites to use real experts on their content (with the usual caveat that this was a small sample, and correlation isn’t causation). Since then, Google has put many of those same observations into writing:.

    Industry observers note that real experts and real lived experiences appear to drive a big share of AI search citations, and you can see it in which sites get cited most. YouTube and Reddit are consistently the two most cited websites in Google’s AI Overviews, at 24.5% and 18.1% of citations among the top 50 cited domains in Ahrefs’ November 2026 analysis.

    Sources indicate that other studies point to LinkedIn, too. In a Semrush study of 325,000 prompts earlier this year, LinkedIn was the second most cited domain in ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode, and Perplexity, and 59% of the LinkedIn content cited in ChatGPT Search and AI Mode came from individual members rather than organization pages.

    Recent findings suggest that this doesn’t surprise me – I’ve seen my LinkedIn posts and Pulse articles show up in Google’s AI search results immediately after publishing, like this test I did with a LinkedIn Pulse article about Google Discover. It earned the top ranking in AI Overviews and an AI Mode citation within seven hours of publishing.

    In other words, a lot of the information AI search systems draw on to build responses comes from the places where real humans go to share what they actually know, like a creator on YouTube walking through how they fixed something or which product they like best, a Reddit thread full of firsthand experience, or a practitioner’s thoughtful LinkedIn post or Pulse article. Unfortunately, these same platforms are also being flooded with AI slop, and it’s not a secret.

    Sources indicate that youTube and Reddit have been fairly explicit about what they want, and it also points to authentic human experiences. In July 2025, YouTube renamed its “repetitious content” monetization rule to “inauthentic content,” covering AI-generated videos made from generic templates “without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective,” and CEO Neal Mohan’s 2026 letter called out “AI slop” by name. Reddit CEO Steve Huffman wrote in February that “if you can’t easily distinguish a real person’s thoughts or recommendations from a bot, that trust erodes,” and a month later Reddit started labeling automated accounts. On both platforms, the most reliable path to visibility appears to be the one this whole post is about: be a real, identifiable person – sharing authentic and honest experiences – whom other people choose to trust.

    I’ve seen firsthand what sharing publicly can do for a business. When I joined Amsive, I had never given an SEO talk on a stage or done anything public-facing in the industry. Since then, in almost nine years on the agency’s SEO team, I’ve published research on its blog under my own name, alongside podcast interviews, conference talks, webinars, and other marketing efforts on the agency’s behalf. That work has brought the agency links, traffic, and name recognition that keep growing long after each piece goes live. When I recently looked at the agency’s backlinks in Ahrefs, a few things stood out:.

    I’m sharing this because of where those links point: every one of them goes to the company. One person (or a team of people) sharing what they know under their own names can grow a company’s authority in a way that brand content on its own rarely does. I’ve seen the same pattern at countless other brands that put trusted experts at the front of their marketing, and I try to employ this same approach in my client strategies.

    Of course, I’m not the only example of this, and others in the industry are seeing success with the same approach. For years, Wix had what the Ahrefs blog called “a bit of a bad reputation for SEO.” Plenty of SEOs would have steered clients away from it. Then Wix did something smart: it hired respected SEOs like Crystal Carter and Mordy Oberstein to represent the brand within the SEO community.

    Industry observers note that crystal joined in 2022, and since then she has spoken at many major search and marketing conferences, co-hosted Wix’s SERP’s Up podcast, and published her own research on the Wix site. Today, when SEO publications write about whether Wix is good for SEO, they often point to her by name. That same Ahrefs article credits her and Mordy with pushing for “more SEO features and better communication.” About 1 in 20 sites linking to Wix’s SEO Hub mention Crystal by name, the podcast demonstrates up in “best SEO podcasts” roundups from Backlinko and Ahrefs, and her expert page is the most-linked expert profile on the hub.

    Industry observers note that for a more famous example outside our industry, look at travel expert Rick Steves. He self-published his first travel guide in 1980, and he has spent about four months a year in Europe for decades, walking the routes himself and updating his guidebooks every year. That one person’s lived experience grew into a company with more than 100 employees, a PBS series that has run since 2000, a thriving forum and online community, a public radio show, and a tour program that takes more than 30,000 travelers to Europe each year.

    I wrote about his site on LinkedIn this summer, calling it the ultimate embodiment of E-E-A-T and the perfect example of an expert-led marketing approach. He tells you – from firsthand experience – what’s overrated, overpriced, or skippable, and because he makes money from books and tours, his content is free from affiliate influence. His honesty is the product. Google’s AI Overviews often cite his website, and his YouTube and TikTok pages too.

    Brands that can should start by identifying the real experts inside the company and investing in making them visible. In practice:.

    Sources indicate that two fair counterpoints, since this approach isn’t possible for every tech giant: Some industries have compliance teams that make personal posting genuinely hard. And people may leave the company and take their personal brands with them. My answer is to try to build several voices instead of relying on one (my friend and colleague Viola Eva recently wrote about how they do exactly this at her company, Flow Agency). Furthermore, remember that any links, mentions, and coverage earned while someone represented the company can remain as valuable assets for the company, even after they move on.

    Recent findings suggest that in July 2023, I posted on LinkedIn that even if Google couldn’t tell AI content from human content, someone else could: “guess who else doesn’t like reading AI content? PEOPLE.” The consumer research has since caught up. A Gartner survey this summer found that a majority of U.S. consumers say AI content has made them less trusting of brand messaging, and Emplifi’s 2026 research found that only 35% of Americans trust AI-generated content at all (not that everyone can necessarily tell the difference). I’d call it slop fatigue, and I think the platforms are finally responding to it (or at least trying to).

    Recent findings suggest that every tactic that has blown up in this industry, from the links I bought in 2011 to the listicles and paid mentions all over the internet in 2026, was scaled for the sole purpose of driving visibility in search. That’s also, almost exactly, the list of things consumers say they dislike most about SEO. Real experts and experienced contributors have the opposite effect: they contribute the things that make the internet human, and the most popular, widely cited platforms are working hard to preserve their humanness in an internet flooded with AI slop.

    It has been revealed that there’s another reason this holds up: your reputation is ultimately decided by what other people say about you, not by what you say about yourself. One of the rater guideline passages I put on a slide back in 2019 reads: “When there is disagreement between what the website says about itself and what reputable independent sources say about the website, we’ll trust the independent sources.”.

    AI search is carrying that torch forward, as LLMs are getting better and better at determining someone’s reputation based on what others say about the brand or the person. That appears to increasingly include spotting self-promotion. Gemini now demonstrates its reasoning steps, and in this example (h/t Gagan Ghotra), it directly evaluated whether “Best AI SEO agency” lists were self-promotional, with agencies ranking themselves highly, to judge how objective those rankings were. Being genuinely recommended by other people is the most sustainable way forward.

    In a recent development, people like following people. That was true before Google, and it’ll still be true after whatever comes next. The brands that figure that out won’t need the next loophole.

    This post was originally published on Lily Ray NYC Substack.

    Industry News: Election season lifted public radio sites. So did a Supreme Court scandal and license plate drama.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • It has been revealed that we will never sell your address.
    • According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    It has been revealed that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Stations in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

    In a recent development, more than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Latest Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

    The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

    Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. Newly introduced Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also key to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total people are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.     Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. Latest Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier.

    “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said.

    “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added.

    Industry observers note that on the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.”.

    BREAKING: Fearless reporting by Fresh Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp.

    — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026.

    WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September.

    Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped.

    “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.”.

    “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also key to take advantage when it delivers,” she added.

    Sources indicate that those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell remarked.

    Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.”.

    The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15.

    In a recent development, according to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary.

    “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.”.

    Recent findings suggest that and then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.”.

    If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers.

    It has been revealed that “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.”.

    Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah.

    Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill.

    According to recent reports, all in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill remarked. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case.

    Industry observers note that “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

    Recent findings suggest that two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

    Industry observers note that “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

    • Industry observers note that on Nov.
    • It has been revealed that benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase.
    • Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said “Goodbye SEO” on X, promoting Palmata, an AI-based tool for tracking how visible a firm is in AI answers, while a Salesforce guide linked on Palmata’s page states SEO “is still the foundation.”.

    It has been revealed that benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase. The post further states, “No click. No referral. Nothing in your analytics,” and then pitches Palmata as a tool that monitors what AI assistants say about a business, offers recommendations on what changes need to be made, and simulates the effect of those changes prior to publication.

    Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.

    In a recent development, salesforce’s guide to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) notes SEO “isn’t going away” and that “SEO is still the foundation.” Graham Hardt, whose byline lists him as SEO Senior Director, wrote it for new businesses, and Salesforce published it Sept. 11. Palmata’s product page links to the guide from its FAQ.

    In a recent development, contentful introduced Palmata in June; it became a part of Salesforce when Salesforce’s acquisition of Contentful occurred on Sept. 1. The article announcing the launch of Palmata, written by Jason McGhee, head of product and engineering for Palmata, said that SEO gave organizations “a practical framework for improving visibility” and added, “That work remains essential.”.

    Aleyda Solis, an SEO and AI search consultant who founded Orainti, wrote in a quote post that AI search “relies on many of the same fundamentals as SEO.” Her post continues, “AI search optimization goes beyond traditional SEO, but it certainly doesn’t replace it.”.

    Solis also wrote that measuring AI search visibility matters, “but monitoring what AI platforms say about your brand and actually improving your visibility, recommendations and business outcomes are very different things.”.

    It has been revealed that pedro Dias, a technical SEO product manager who used to work at Google, wrote that SEO “was never a topic that attracted the interest of decision makers.” His post adds, “SEO isn’t traffic. It never has been.”.

    Lily Ray, who founded Algorythmic, replied to Benioff, “This gold rush already happened and the market is already oversaturated.” Growth advisor Eli Schwartz wrote that “there’s yet another AEO tool in the mix.”.

    When Benioff’s post is read by a marketing executive, Salesforce’s own guide answers it, stating that SEO and AEO are “two visibility layers for the same audience.”.

    In terms of making the case for fresh businesses to include both SEO and AEO, this guide provides Salesforce’s reasoning for including SEO in your plans right alongside any AI visibility tool, such as Palmata.

    Industry observers note that according to Palmata’s FAQ section, Palmata is a standalone tool that is also built into Marketing Cloud by Salesforce. In weighing tools like Palmata, Salesforce’s guide says you should track “both sets of metrics.” This means tracking your organic traffic and rankings, but also tracking how many times you’ve been cited by AI.

    Latest Update: WordPress Random Redirects, Branded API Data & CDN Advice – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, new data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.
    • It has been revealed that wordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API.
    • WordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, new data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.

    It has been revealed that wordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API. Google also published the referrer values its traffic sends and shared ways in which a CDN move could lead to blocking Googlebot. Ask Maps began contacting local businesses, and United Airlines included its AI agent rules within its terms.

    Here’s what matters for you and your work.

    WordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec. 8, contains a new feature called /random/, turned on by default, to send a visitor to a randomly selected published post. There is no option in the dashboard settings for this to be turned off.

    Key facts: According to the developer note, /random/ randomly selects posts and also custom post types as long as they are publicly queryable and have archives (unless the developer has registered them using 'randomable' => false) and excludes pages and attachments. The development code uses a 302 status code along with an X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow HTTP header when it redirects the visitor but does not send that header on the post that the visitor arrives at. To turn the feature off, developers need the wp_enable_random_content_redirect filter, and the different spelling given in WordPress’s November developer news roundup isn’t found anywhere in the code.

    In a recent development, testimonials for clients (and other custom post type entries) may never be accessed via navigation. When their post type is eligible, they can be reached through /random/, even if they have been set to noindex by an SEO plugin. Before you update, check which post types would meet WordPress’s eligibility criteria, and ask a developer to exclude those that should not show up.

    It has been revealed that read our full coverage: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made.

    Teams using the Search Console API can now segment the data they pull into branded and non-branded searches without having to maintain a list of their brands as regular expressions (regex).

    Key facts: Three Performance report features were added to the Search Analytics API by Google on Nov. 16. The brandedClassification dimension works only with eligible properties, and according to the API reference, the data provided for this dimension starts on Feb. 21, 2026. Setting type to webMultimodal returns results from Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android and image uploads, and a fresh filterLists field allows you to filter by multiple countries or devices in a single request.

    For reports covering dates before Feb. 21, 2026, you’ll still need your own brand regex. Google’s announcement of the branded queries filter states “some queries may occasionally be misidentified,” so comparing the API split with the regex you already use can help you spot where they differ.

    Read our full coverage: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API.

    A google.com referrer lets you know in your analytics when Google sends a visitor, but it doesn’t show which source (Search, Discover or Google Images) was behind it, claims a fresh Search Central page.

    Industry observers note that key facts: The page was listed Nov. 12 in Google’s documentation updates log. It claims Google Search utilizes an origin referrer policy for its Search results; thus, the header will contain only the scheme and host, and not the search query. Referrers from Discover carry the values of the surface where Discover was viewed. Same-origin services such as Google Images send the same values as Search and Discover.

    Industry observers note that to distinguish Discover clicks from Search clicks, use Search Console’s Discover report rather than referrer data. If Google traffic appears as referral or direct in your analytics, Google’s page recommends checking whether custom channel rules, referral exclusions, or filters are reclassifying it.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Find Search Traffic In Analytics & Logs.

    A CDN can let Googlebot crawl your site faster before the CDN’s cache has filled, according to Google, and those requests then go to your origin server.

    Sources indicate that key facts: On Nov. 11, Search Central posted Google’s explanation that a fast and reliable CDN may slowly increase a site’s crawl capacity limit, while a brand new CDN begins with an empty cache. The first visit to each URL is a cache miss, so the page has to come from your origin server, and crawlers visit far more of your site’s URLs than visitors do, with most visitors sticking to a small set of popular pages. When admins block all bots from their site using blanket bot protection, they can cause Googlebot to fail CAPTCHA challenges. If this stays in place, then the pages of the site begin to drop out of search results.

    It has been revealed that google’s advice for the move is to allow verified bots in the CDN and firewall settings, then pre-warm caches by fetching your most popular and frequently crawled URLs before switching traffic. Before enabling bot protection during the migration, be sure the verified-bot setting is turned on.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems.

    Recent findings suggest that google’s Ask Maps has started calling some U.S. beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses to identify available appointment times for customers.

    Recent findings suggest that key facts: On Nov. 16 a post from Google said that customers can use Ask Maps to find these appointments online and have it call local businesses, then see available time slots so the customer can decide where to book. The feature started rolling out on Android and iOS, with the ability to find appointments launching in the U.S. first. Google already makes automated calls to businesses for customers using Google Search and Maps, including booking appointments and confirming availability, and this process is covered in Google’s Business Profile help page.

    In Google’s demo, Ask Maps demonstrates four times for a gel manicure that it confirmed were available online.

    The setting Google documents for those automated calls is the “Bookings and inquiries from customers” option in Advanced settings in your verified Business Profile. However, Google’s Ask Maps post does not indicate if calls received via Ask Maps are subject to this setting. Check what you have set, and make sure whoever answers the phone knows these calls come from Google on behalf of a customer.

    Read our full coverage: Google Adds Appointment Finding & Business Calls To Ask Maps.

    United Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov. 11, let search engines index its public pages but require written permission for any AI agent that searches, books or buys on its site or app.

    Key facts: The terms also bar using data from United’s site or app, such as fares and schedules, to “train, fine-tune, ground, evaluate, or otherwise develop” an AI model. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt named no AI crawlers or agents. Separately, HUMAN Security’s October report found that Meta’s and OpenAI’s agents made about 90% of the agent requests on sites and apps it protects.

    In HUMAN Security’s October data, Muse accounted for 59% of agent requests. Three OpenAI agents accounted for about 30% combined.

    Meta’s Muse publishes no user agent for a robots.txt rule to name, as Slobodan Manic wrote in October, so whether it gets in comes down to your terms and bot protection. Muse sent the most requests in HUMAN’s data, and bot rules can check the signatures some of its requests carry, whose key directory DataDome reported had moved to muse.ai by Nov. 9.

    Read our full coverage: United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First and Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data.

    Much of this week’s SEO work sits with teams outside of SEO. The next steps for this week include identifying who is responsible for the off switch for the /random/ redirect, as well as reporting on the branded split and the analytics rules for referrers. Google’s CDN advice should be reviewed by whoever runs the CDN and firewall, and the automated calls toggle is managed through the Business Profile. United’s rules related to agents are contained within a legal agreement. Before the next change, the first step is to determine who has responsibility for each of these in your own organization.

    According to recent reports, our mission is to bring clarity and control to the world's most complex codebases. AI is accelerating code creation, but the infrastructure to understand, oversee, and evolve that code hasn't kept pace. Sourcegraph gives engineering organizations full visibility across their systems, precise context for their agents, and the ability to execute coordinated code changes at scale. As agentic development becomes the dominant engineering paradigm, we provide the context layer teams need to take control of their codebase.With Code Search, Deep Search, MCP, and Agentic Batch Changes, we deliver on that mission today - giving engineering teams and their AI tools the cross-repo context to navigate massive codebases with confidence, and the ability to make changes across hundreds of repositories at once.Companies like Stripe, Reddit, and Leidos rely on Sourcegraph to ship faster and with higher quality. We're backed by a16z, Sequoia, and Redpoint, and proud to operate as a globally distributed team that values high agency, direct communication, and customer love.If you want to build the infrastructure that lets every engineering team - and every agent they deploy - operate on their codebase with confidence, join us.

    🌎 While we hire almost anywhere in the world, we have a preference for someone to reside in the following locations for this role. However, if you feel qualified, we welcome you to apply regardless of location. No matter what, working hours must overlap with Pacific Time for at least 25 hours/week.

    It has been revealed that we are hiring a Sr. Product Marketing Manager to help us tell the Sourcegraph story and scale the go-to-market for one of the most critical pieces of engineering infrastructure for the largest enterprises building the future.In this role, you will report to our Head of Marketing, and sit at the intersection of our go-to-market and technical teams to drive thought leadership, product leadership, and market leadership. Our customers are developers and engineering leaders at the largest and most successful companies in the world who rely on us to help them write better code, understand their codebases, secure their products, and adopt the newest and most impactful technology. You will translate deep technical capability into clear market narratives, turn product direction into rolls out that land, and ensure go-to-market is aligned, credible, and effective.Sourcegraph is a $50m ARR business and growing fast. We are doubling down on our core Search technology, including Deep Search, Code Search, Sourcegraph MCP and APIs for agents, and critical code migration and workflow engines, like Agentic Batch Changes for large-scale changes at scale. You will be responsible for the technical product marketing that will bring that story to life in the market, as well as ensuring alignment with and results from our Demand Gen and DevRel teams.We move fast and hold ourselves to an extremely high bar for product quality and Developer authenticity. If you’ve made a mark in product marketing for developers, talk to us.

You’re equally comfortable shaping narratives that connect with our technical enterprise audience, enabling sales, and shipping debuts that move the business forward. You understand the software development lifecycle and are excited about how AI is reshaping developer tools and workflows.Must-haves:.

    The balance of empathy and compliance: a proven ability to write about highly sensitive personal health topics (menopause symptoms, hormonal changes, wellness) with profound empathy while strictly adhering to healthcare compliance rules and ad-network medical restrictions.

    An experimenter’s ego — you don’t take copy critiques personally. You’re obsessed with letting consumer behavior and performance data crown the winning angle.

    • Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.
    • ProcessOS is a upcoming kind of Camunda product: business processes described in natural language, generated as executable BPMN workflows, and improved autonomously from production data.
    • You’ll work end‑to‑end across Java services and React interfaces, collaborating closely with a talented global team to measure, improve, and scale performance and fault tolerance in real-world distributed systems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    ProcessOS is a upcoming kind of Camunda product: business processes described in natural language, generated as executable BPMN workflows, and improved autonomously from production data. We’re hiring the first cohort of Forward Deployed Engineers to bring it into production at enterprise customers. You’ll own the deployment journey from first process file to a working, improving system, and hand off a functioning capability to the customer’s team. The code you write and the patterns you discover feed directly back into how ProcessOS is built. This is a rare opportunity to shape a product, a function, and a field practice from day one.

    You’ll work end‑to‑end across Java services and React interfaces, collaborating closely with a talented global team to measure, improve, and scale performance and fault tolerance in real-world distributed systems.

    Deploy and prove. Own the journey from first process file to production workflow. At 90 days: at least one workflow running, the improvement loop active, and measurable fitness gains the customer can see. At 12 months: 3–5 customers with viable deployments.

    Drive organizational adoption. Work across technical and business stakeholders to build understanding and trust, turning early deployments into lasting customer capability.

    Industry observers note that work at depth technically. Configure and run Camunda clusters locally and in cloud environments. Debug integration failures. Build custom agents where platform defaults don’t fit. Write connector logic that gets legacy enterprise systems talking to ProcessOS.

    Industry observers note that build the playbook. There is no deployment template yet. Document what good looks like as you discover it, and make the next implementation faster.

    Industry observers note that feed the product. Custom agents you write get contributed back. Integration patterns get codified. Production bugs you find, you often fix. Your field work is a direct input to ProcessOS.

    In a recent development, hand off deliberately. Leave customers with a team that can operate independently, is trained on the platform, and acts on improvement results without you.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    According to recent reports, enterprise production experience: you’ve shipped something inside a large organization and stayed to see it operate. You know why governance and resilience matter at scale.

    Technical depth: You can debug an integration failure, write a custom agent against a legacy API, stand up a Camunda cluster from scratch, and explain generated BPMN to both engineers and business leads.

    Stakeholder communication: you work effectively across engineering, architecture, and business leadership and adapt how you communicate without losing precision.

    Practical AI experience: you’ve used AI to solve real problems in production – not just experimented. You understand context management, prompt engineering, agent testing, and integration tradeoffs.

    Comfort with ambiguity: you make sound judgment calls without a playbook and document what you learn.

    Occasional travel may be required.

    Experience in a customer-facing engineering or professional services role.

    Familiarity with regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare, or insurance.

    Production experience with agentic systems or AI-integrated workflows.

    Contributions to a shared platform or open source project that others built on.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    Industry observers note that we offer competitive, fair, and transparent compensation. Salary ranges are location-based, with Standard and Major markets (global tech hubs) reflecting local competition.

    The Annual Total Target Cash (base salary + 100% variable target, where applicable) shown below spans from the minimum in a Standard market to the maximum in a Major market.     United States: $157,300.00 to $253,600.00.

    United Kingdom: £98,800.00 to £162,400.00.

    Singapore: S$195,400.00 to S$293,000.00.

    If you’re based elsewhere, you’ll be hired via Remote.com (our global employer partner), and your Talent Acquisition Partner will provide a personalized Total Rewards Calculator after your first interview.

    Equity: We also offer equity (where applicable) through our Virtual Stock Option Plan (VSOP).

    We invest in your wellbeing, growth, and ability to connect, along with perks that support you no matter where you’re based. Our benefits are globally designed and locally delivered where applicable.

    Remote & Flexible: Work from anywhere with the setup that suits you, home office budget, co-working space support, and flexible time off to recharge when you need it.

    In Person Connection: We invest in meaningful face time through our Annual Kickoff (Vienna in 2025, Madrid in 2026!), team offsites, and Camundi Connection Budgets, including contributing to meetups while travelling,, and local gatherings with fellow Camundi.

    Health & Wellbeing: Access locally tailored healthcare, Modern Health for global mental wellbeing, and our Live Well Lifestyle Spending Account (LSA), a flexible, global benefit that puts you in control of your whole life, not just work, from: staying active, to caring for family, exploring personal passions, meaningful experiences, and investing in your financial wellbeing. The Live Well program launches in 2026 and scales to €1,000 annually from 2027.

    Financial Security: Retirement and pension plans (often with company contributions), plus life and disability insurance where relevant.

    Professional Growth: Up to $/€/£1,000 per year for self-driven learning: courses, certifications, books, you decide!

    AI in our hiring process: Camunda may use AI tools to aid the screening of applications and during the interview process. You can learn more here.

    ”Everyone is welcome at Camunda” — it’s a celebrated component of our culture. We strive to create an inclusive environment that empowers our people. At Camunda, we honour diverse cultures and backgrounds and are proud to be an equal opportunity employer. All qualified applicants will receive consideration without regard to gender, race, ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, age, disability or any other protected characteristics under applicable law. We are looking forward to your application!

    Come join us and be part of Camunda’s incredible journey: Make an impact at a pivotal moment in our story!

    Please be aware that scammers may impersonate Camunda by reaching out about job opportunities. We will never ask candidates for bank account details, checks, payment, or other sensitive financial information as part of our hiring process.     Senior Forward Deployed Engineer at Clutch

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions.
    • In a recent development, as a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent.
    • This is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions. Emma, our collections agent, is live at five credit unions and handled 60,000+ member conversations in her first twelve weeks at one of them. Behind her is a growing portfolio: origination, fraud step-up, member (re)engagement and activation agents, all built on the same Agents Platform (TypeScript, NestJS, our own agent SDK, MCP, Temporal, promptfoo).

    In a recent development, as a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent. You take it from "sold" to "live and performing" at a specific credit union: you sit in the discovery sessions, you build the integrations to their core banking and loan systems, you author and tune the agent's behavior, you run the live tests with their staff, and you stay with it through go-live and the first weeks of production. When something needs a person in the room, you are the one who flies.

    This is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role. You write production code in our monorepo every week: integrations, modules, and the agents themselves (prompts, tools, evals), together with the other engineers on the pod. The difference from a traditional engineer is that you are on site more often, you make judgment calls in front of the customer, and you own the outcome. What you learn in the field flows straight back into the product: defaults, playbooks, and the platform capabilities the next agent will need.

    Recent findings suggest that you build; our AI Operations Managers deliver. The pod (pod lead plus engineers) designs and builds each agent in a high-touch way with the first customers. Once the agent is defined and live, AI Ops coordinates the implementations, configuration and ongoing success at the next credit unions. You hand them something that works and a playbook to run it.

    In a recent development, this role requires roughly 20% of travel on average, with one- to two-week stretches around kickoffs and go-lives. Based in the US, able to travel on short notice.

    You'll join the Agents team, a small, senior group operating as a startup inside Clutch: seven engineers, a dedicated AI product group, and AI sales specialists, working directly with some of the largest credit unions in the country. Every agent is staffed by a pair of engineers, one leaning toward the conversation and LLM side, one toward software and integrations, with a pod lead who owns the product day to day. There is no layer between you and the customer, and no layer between you and the platform team.

    Recent findings suggest that the operating style is direct, written, and evidence-driven: BLUF updates, evals over opinions, business outcomes over ticket counts. The team is spread across Brazil, Argentina and the US and works async by default. Being on site is a tool we use at specific moments (kickoff, live testing, go-live), not a permanent posting.

    Ship your first production change to a live agent through the team's review process, and be able to explain how a member's call flows through the Agents Platform end to end.

    Learn one agent deeply: system prompt, tool contracts, orchestration triggers, compliance gates, and the implementation process from kickoff to go-live.

    Join at least one credit union implementation as the second engineer, including a live testing session with their staff.

    Map where the current implementation process loses time and where a default or a tool would have removed a round trip.

    Own the technical side of one credit union implementation end to end: core and LOS integration, agent configuration, testing, go-live, and the first weeks of production.

    Run the eval and tuning loop for your agent (golden transcripts, rubric judges, regression suite) and be trusted to change its behavior without a second engineer checking your work.

    Have completed at least two on-site visits and turned what you heard there into product decisions with your pod lead and PM.

    Contribute at least one reusable capability back to the Agents Platform that the next implementation will not have to rebuild.

    Have taken one net-new agent from sold to live at its first credit union, with data you can show the partner.

    Be the engineer credit union staff ask for by name when something in their deployment needs to change.

    Have written the implementation playbook for your agent well enough that the AI Ops team runs the second and third credit union without you.

    Be shaping what the next agents look like, because you have seen where the current ones break in the field.

    Recent findings suggest that 7+ years of software engineering in a fast-paced environment, preferably in SaaS and/or Fintech, with senior TypeScript and Node.js backend experience in a large codebase (NestJS, CQRS, schema-validated boundaries, dependency injection). We do not count years of AI experience; the field is too young for that to mean anything. We look at what you have shipped and how you reason about it.

    Integration and API engineering: secure service-to-service endpoints, third-party APIs, webhooks, and the patience to work with legacy banking systems that were not designed to be integrated.

    Security and auth judgment: OAuth and machine-to-machine auth, tenant-scoped access, secrets handling, no PII in logs. Our agents touch sensitive member data and operate under consumer-contact regulation.

    It has been revealed that customer presence: you can sit across from a VP of Collections, hear a request, and say "here is what I recommend and why", including when the answer is no. You are comfortable making calls in the room and owning them afterwards.

    Code-quality judgment under deadline pressure: you take on debt deliberately, name it, and pay it down, rather than gold-plating or leaving silent debt behind.

    In a recent development, genuine appetite for LLM agents: eval discipline for non-deterministic systems, reading a system prompt like code, understanding that some decisions must never reach the model. Curiosity plus shipped work is enough; research depth is not required.
